# Background

A review of the `ramb` package on 2026-10-12 found that distance between two points was computed
in five places, on two different definitions of the Earth:

| Implementation | Location | Definition | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rb_calc_distance()` | `R/track.R` | Haversine, sphere R = 6,371,000 m | users, `.rb_whack_fwdbwd()` (data frames), `.rb_whack_duplicates()` |
| `.rb_geodesic()` | `R/track.R` | Vincenty inverse, WGS84 ellipsoid | `rb_calc_speed()`, `rb_calc_step_acceleration()` |
| C++ Haversine | `src/whack_forward.cpp`, `src/whack_sda.cpp` | Haversine, same sphere | the impossible-position filters |
| Inline SQL Haversine | `R/whack.R` | Haversine, same sphere | `.rb_whack_fwdbwd()` on lazy DuckDB tables |
| `ST_Distance` | `R/trip.R` (trip stays) | planar, in degrees | nearest-port ranking |

Two consequences followed. Speeds were computed on the ellipsoid while the impossible-position
filters judged them on the sphere, so a ping could pass a `kn_max` filter yet compute as
over-threshold. And `rb_calc_distance()` — the user-facing distance function — exposed only one
of the two definitions.

This report records what was changed in the session of 2026-10-12, the measurements behind the
choice of default method, the DuckDB macro exploration, and the reconciliation with the earlier
design direction in fishycode plan 013.

# What was built

Committed as `3afe1f2` (implementation) and `96182b0` (contributor notes):

- `rb_calc_distance()` gained `method = c("haversine", "geodesic")`. The default Haversine path
  is bit-identical to before; `"geodesic"` routes to the WGS84 engine.
- Vincenty's formula now tracks per-pair convergence: nearly antipodal pairs warn and fall back
  to Haversine instead of silently returning the 200th iterate.
- A data-frame form: the first argument may be a data frame, with tidy-eval coordinate columns.
- `rb_calc_speed()` and `rb_calc_step_acceleration()` gained the same `method` argument, with
  the default flipped from geodesic to haversine — one sphere across distance, speed and the
  filters.
- Each Haversine copy (R, two C++, the SQL) now carries a comment naming `rb_calc_distance()`
  as the reference of record.

The package is loaded from its development sources for the examples below:

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
devtools::load_all("/Users/einarhj/R/Pakkar/ramb", quiet = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: api-demo
# the vector form (positional or named), unchanged
rb_calc_distance(-21.93, 64.15, -23.93, 65.65)

# the data-frame form: distance from each ping to a fixed port
d <- data.frame(
  lon = c(-21.93, -22.50),
  lat = c(64.15, 63.90),
  port_lon = -21.94,
  port_lat = 64.15
)
rb_calc_distance(d, lon2 = port_lon, lat2 = port_lat)
rb_calc_distance(d, lon2 = port_lon, lat2 = port_lat, method = "geodesic")
```

# Choosing the default method

## The error surface

The relative difference between the Haversine sphere and the WGS84 ellipsoid was measured on
north–south and east–west legs at several latitudes:

```{r}
#| label: error-surface
rel_diff <- function(lat, km, bearing = c("N", "E")) {
  bearing <- match.arg(bearing)
  deg_per_km <- 1 / 111.32
  if (bearing == "N") {
    lon1 <- 0; lat1 <- lat; lon2 <- 0; lat2 <- lat + km * deg_per_km
  } else {
    lon1 <- 0; lat1 <- lat; lon2 <- km * deg_per_km; lat2 <- lat
  }
  h <- rb_calc_distance(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2)
  g <- rb_calc_distance(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2, method = "geodesic")
  (h - g) / g * 100
}

lat <- c(0, 30, 55, 64, 70, 80)
grid <- expand.grid(lat = lat, km = 1)
data.frame(
  lat = grid$lat,
  north = mapply(rel_diff, grid$lat, grid$km, bearing = "N"),
  east  = mapply(rel_diff, grid$lat, grid$km, bearing = "E")
) |> round(3)
```

The error is essentially independent of leg length (it is a radius mismatch, not noise) and is
systematic: bounded within about ±0.6 % everywhere — worst at the equator going north–south
(`{r} rel_diff(0, 1, "N") |> round(2)` %) and at 80° N (`{r} rel_diff(80, 1, "N") |> round(2)` %)
— and roughly ±0.1–0.3 % at mid-to-high latitudes. *(Corrected 2026-10-13: at Icelandic latitudes, 63–67° N, it has one sign — the haversine distance is shorter by 0.24 % on north–south legs to 0.40 % on east–west ones.)* Being systematic, it does not cancel in
summed distances such as track kilometres or effort.

## Execution speed

On ten million point pairs:

```{r}
#| label: benchmark
set.seed(6421)
n <- 1e7
lon1 <- runif(n, -180, 180)
lat1 <- runif(n, -85, 85)
lon2 <- lon1 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.05)
lat2 <- pmin(85, pmax(-85, lat1 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.05)))

t_hav <- system.time(.rb_haversine(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2))[["elapsed"]]
t_geo <- system.time(.rb_geodesic(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2))[["elapsed"]]
c(haversine = t_hav, geodesic = t_geo, ratio = t_geo / t_hav)
```

Haversine ran in `{r} round(t_hav, 2)` s against `{r} round(t_geo, 2)` s for the ellipsoid —
about `{r} round(t_geo / t_hav)` times slower. Haversine is one closed-form vectorised
expression; the ellipsoid method is iterative and runs until every pair converges. Haversine is
also the only method that exists in all three backends (R, C++, SQL).

## The decision

The default is `"haversine"` everywhere: one sphere (R = 6,371,000 m) across distance, speed
and the impossible-position filters. The ellipsoid error at track-step sizes sits below AIS
position noise (~10 m on a 1 km step is 1 %), while consistency with the filters is exact and
free. `method = "geodesic"` remains for when the absolute distance itself matters — the
systematic bias does not cancel in sums.

# The SQL macro exploration

A natural next question was whether a DuckDB SQL macro (registered per connection) should carry
the vectorised functions into `tbl_lazy` queries. A proof of concept worked mechanically, but
surfaced a semantic trap worth recording:

```{r}
#| label: duckdb-least-null
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT LEAST(1, NULL) AS least_ignores_null")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

DuckDB's `LEAST()` and `GREATEST()` ignore NULLs. A Haversine macro clamped with
`LEAST(1, ...)` — the guard R needs against floating-point overshoot — would silently turn a
NULL coordinate into the antipodal distance (~20,015 km) instead of NULL. The existing inline
SQL in the filters is unclamped, so NULL propagates correctly there.

The advice in session was to not build the macro: one SQL call site, per-connection registration
bookkeeping, and Haversine-only (an iterative method is not a SQL expression). That advice was
later retracted in part — see the next section.

# Reconciliation with plan 013

After the build, the fishycode tracker `curate/plans/013-ramb-one-flow.md` was re-read. Its
"One distance function" section (maintainer's direction, 2026-10-09, written before anything
was built) prescribes a design that differs from what was built:

| Plan 013 direction (2026-10-09) | Built 2026-10-12 |
|---|---|
| `method = c("geodesic", "andoyer", "haversine")`, geodesic default | two methods, haversine default |
| Karney via vendored GeographicLib C (Rcpp), replacing Vincenty, which was ruled out for failing silently near the antipode | Vincenty kept, with warning + Haversine fallback |
| `rb_register_macros(con)` + a `rb_calc_distance` DuckDB macro; lazy geodesic via `ST_Distance_Spheroid`; mechanics already designed and measured | not built; lazy input errors clearly |
| filters switch to exact after a counted-change study | filters stay Haversine; speed moved to the filters' sphere instead |

A decision record (080) was drafted for fishycode recording what was built, the deviations and
their session rationale, and what remains open — deferred, not cancelled:

- the Karney engine (the real fix for the antipode; re-opens if distance-steamed totals become
  a published product, since the sphere's bias does not cancel in sums);
- the `"andoyer"` method and `rb_register_macros()`;
- the counted filter switch to exact distances;
- the trip-stays nearest-port ranking, still planar `ST_Distance` in degrees (already a row in
  plan 013's logic-question table).

# Next steps

The agreed next step within ramb is the Karney engine: vendor GeographicLib-C v2.2's
`geodesic.c`/`geodesic.h` unchanged into `src/` (MIT/X11, attribution in DESCRIPTION and
`inst/COPYRIGHTS`), expose `geod_inverse()` through one Rcpp entry point, and swap
`.rb_geodesic()` over — removing Vincenty and the fallback machinery. The plan also covers
verification against `traipse` (including the antipode and the near-antipodal pair where
Vincenty was measured 7,059 m short), a scale test on the June 2023 legs from the fishycode
parquet store, and the test/docs/NEWS updates. After that, the `jepol` voyage-cutting
off-by-one, which plan 013 assigns to ramb as its own commit.

Two smaller loose ends remain on the fishycode side, for when it next updates ramb: the local
`hav()` copy in `curate/checks/whack_floor_measure.R` can be replaced by `rb_calc_distance()`,
and the `speed` column in `curate/ais_ping_union.R` shifts ~0.1–0.3 % with the new haversine
default — pin `method = "geodesic"` there or re-run, by decision. *(Corrected 2026-10-13: the shift is
0.24–0.40 %, always downward; fishycode decision 080 took haversine, named in the call.)*
